implementation_notes: Akka provides the channel as a classifier-keyed event bus: subscribe(subscriber, classifier), unsubscribe and publish are the three operations, and the bundled LookupClassification or SubchannelClassification map a classifier extracted from each event - a topic string or the event's class, including subclasses - to the subscriber set. In an actor system context.system.eventStream is already such a bus for application events, subscribed to with subscribe(self, classOf[Event]), which keeps subscribers in the actor model and its supervision. publish dispatches synchronously, so actor subscribers get mailbox decoupling while plain callbacks block the publisher.
code_sketch:
class LookupBusImpl extends EventBus with LookupClassification {
  type Event = MsgEnvelope; type Classifier = String; type Subscriber = ActorRef
  protected def classify(event: Event): Classifier = event.topic
  protected def publish(event: Event, subscriber: Subscriber): Unit = subscriber ! event.payload
  protected def compareSubscribers(a: Subscriber, b: Subscriber): Int = a.compareTo(b)
  protected def mapSize(): Int = 128
}

bus.subscribe(dashboard, "price")
bus.publish(MsgEnvelope("price", Price("MSFT", 83.0)))
pitfalls: publish runs on the publisher's thread: non-actor subscribers execute inline and can block the publisher.
Actor subscriptions do not survive a restart unless they are re-established in preStart/postStop.
The classic EventBus does not preserve the original sender - carry it inside the event if consumers need a reply address.

variants.name: ZIO Hub (publish/subscribe)
variants.idiom_name: Hub[A].publish / Hub[A].subscribe returning a scoped Dequeue
variants.implementation_notes: In ZIO the channel is Hub[A]: publish sends to every subscriber, subscribe returns a scoped Dequeue whose subscription is removed when the scope closes, and the constructor encodes the overflow policy - bounded backpressures publishers, dropping and sliding drop, unbounded never blocks but can grow without limit. ZStream.fromHub turns each subscription into an ordinary stream, so subscribers are pipelines and the subscription lifetime is the scope's lifetime rather than a manual unsubscribe. Choose it when the application is already effect-based; otherwise the Akka bus or a plain listener list is closer to the metal.
pitfalls: A subscriber only sees events published while its subscription scope is open; racing publish against subscribe loses messages unless a Promise gates the subscription.
A bounded hub backpressures the publisher, so one slow subscriber reduces the publish rate for everyone (dropping/sliding trade delivery for isolation).
Unbounded hubs are the only policy that guarantees both full delivery and a non-blocking publisher, at the risk of unbounded memory.
